The day before we spoke, King1, 26, had learned that his friend Lamont had been killed. He was at home when his cousin called to break the news and asked him to come over. ‘I’m on my way,’ King replied immediately, knowing what was being asked of him. He ran up to his room to retrieve his Glock, opened his box of bullets and, one by one, filled the clip.

Lamont was dead, though King couldn’t fully wrap his mind around the fact. He’d seen him only hours earlier, when Lamont and King’s cousin stopped by his house. They’d been shot at by their rivals the day before, and King had warned them to be careful: ‘Y’all need to keep y’alls’ heads up.’ Now the car Lamont died in sat empty on a nearby street, shot up and stained with his blood. King watched a video posted on Facebook of paramedics draping the body with a sheet and carrying it into an ambulance.

King knew what came next. He and his cousin would go out with their guns and ride through the neighbourhood until they found the men responsible. ‘I just wanted my get-back,’ he said. He wanted the people who killed Lamont to feel what he was feeling. And if he couldn’t find them, he’d find someone else he had beef with. King reasoned: ‘It could be a person who I don’t like or who I’m already into it with. I’m going to slide on them too and whoever else. That’s how I grew up with my feelings. That’s how I let off my rage.’

To King, retaliation felt less like a choice than an inevitability. ‘Whether I do it or not, somebody going to do it,’ he said. ‘If it ain’t me, I got other homies who feel the same way I feel. I got cousins, family members, they mommas. That’s how it be, and that’s how it’s going to always be. It’s a repeated cycle.’
His clip was full. Then King decided to do something that a year earlier he would not have done.

For King, and for many Americans like him, gun violence is not an exceptional event but a fact of life. In some parts of the United States, lethal violence has reached a scale exceeding recent wars and military occupations. Between 2020 and 2021, a young man in Chicago’s Garfield Park neighbourhood, where King is from, faced a higher risk of being killed than a US soldier deployed to Afghanistan or Iraq. By age 40, around half of the city’s Black and Hispanic residents will have witnessed someone being shot.

Violent crime has fallen steeply across the US since 2021, though not everywhere. According to Chicago’s crime dashboard, fatal shootings in Chicago were up 7 per cent this year as of late September. But even in cities where the decline has held, a citywide figure is a poor description of how violence is experienced. In US cities, most shootings concentrate in a few dozen blocks and among a few hundred people who account for less than 1 per cent of a city’s population. Thus, citywide numbers cannot capture what it is like to live inside that zone, where violence is not a discrete event but an experience that leaves stubborn traces on many lives.

In 2022, I was part of a research team that interviewed 99 men from Chicago’s highest-violence neighbourhoods. All were former or current participants in the Rapid Employment and Development Initiative, or READI Chicago, a community violence intervention run by a partnership of Heartland Alliance, the University of Chicago and seven nonprofit organisations on the city’s south and west sides. READI served adult men at greatest risk of shooting someone or being shot. By the time they entered the programme, 98 per cent had been arrested, averaging more than 17 times each, and 35 per cent had been shot. For 18 months, participants were paid to work and attend group cognitive behavioural intervention (CBI) sessions. Outreach workers helped them navigate housing, legal, safety and substance-use crises that might otherwise have made steady participation difficult.
The men had learned to anticipate danger in ordinary moments and to meet it by fighting back

We asked each person we spoke with to tell us the story of his life, then to reconstruct minor confrontations, conflicts averted, and those that escalated into violence. We asked what they had been thinking and feeling as these events unfolded, returning to a single question: ‘What was going through your mind when that happened?’ Our aim was to access a layer of cognition beneath the behaviour, and to understand how the men made sense of their own actions and those of others.

Our conversations revealed something important about what violence teaches the mind. Lives spent amid violence meant the men had learned to anticipate danger in ordinary moments and to meet it by fighting back. The premise of READI’s work, and our research, is that because this way of seeing was learned, it could also be unlearned.

The danger these men read into the world is real; recall that more than a third of them had been shot. The difficulty is that a mind shaped by real danger does not confine its lessons to dangerous situations. It brings them into ambiguous ones, where the reading is wrong often enough to produce the very danger it anticipates. The outer world and the inner one are not separate. A world of violence sustains itself not only through guns, poverty and other social ills, but also through the ways of seeing it produces. Our research asks where these patterns of seeing and responding come from, why they persist, and how they can change.
Again and again, three patterns surfaced that could make future violence more likely.

The first was misreading situations. A great deal of violence, the men told us, stems from misconstruing some aspect of an interpersonal interaction, such as the nature of the situation or the other person’s intent. Past experiences of violence had created threat-oriented frames that quickly registered ambiguous cues as dangerous. Nuke, 24, told us that even a stranger looking at him for too long could escalate into a confrontation: ‘Sometimes I’ll react. Like: “Man, what the fuck is you looking at?”’

Tim, now 30, traced this reactive impulse to being shot and nearly killed at 17. ‘I was young in the streets, so I was always an impulsive person,’ he recalled. ‘But it got really bad after [I was shot]. I felt like the world was against me … If you approach me a certain type of way and if you wasn’t a person I was with on a daily basis, I felt like you was my enemy.’ Even casual remarks became charged: ‘Before that incident, I’ll be like: “Man, whatever.” But now it’s like: “Man, what you mean by that?… You saying that you going to shoot me?”’ Like many others we spoke with, Tim had lost loved ones to gun violence and had been shot at himself. But a mind tuned to danger could also misread ordinary situations, reproducing the violence that had trained it.

The second pattern was a narrowing of perceived response options. When violence seemed possible, those we spoke with often saw only a narrow set of things they could do. Kobe, 24, described the months after his release from prison: ‘I was walking around like a ticking time bomb. Soon as somebody did anything, I’m whooping them like I’m they daddy.’ Similarly, when King learned that Lamont was dead, his thoughts narrowed to one response: revenge.

Such narrowing can be adaptive in dangerous situations, where hesitation can be costly. But when it is applied more generally, it can lead to serious problems. In these moments, people tend to bypass deliberate reflection and may feel that certain responses are inevitable, as King told us: ‘That’s how it be, and that’s how it’s going to always be. It’s a repeated cycle.’

Third, our interviews revealed that participants often read violent behaviour as proof of who someone was, rather than how that person had responded to a situation. Psychologists call this the fundamental attribution error, or our tendency to explain behaviour through features of a person’s character rather than circumstance. But the men turned this error most mercilessly on themselves.
Accepting violence as part of who they were made their future involvement in violence more likely

Take William, who had lost 11 close friends to gun violence by the age of 29. He came to see revenge not as something he did but as something he was. ‘I ain’t been a civilian since I was like eight…,’ he told us. ‘To sleep at night [with what I’ve done] you got to be a different type of monster.’ After his best friend was killed, he said: ‘I bought guns, a lot of them … I wasn’t going to feel safe until somebody was dead.’ Over time, the identity hardened: ‘To put that bet on somebody else, you got to be a cold-hearted motherfucker. Melatonin can’t even help you sleep after that.’

Terrel, 29, had endured a childhood of compounding losses. His mother was incarcerated, his little sister killed in a house fire, and he was shot – all before finishing the eighth grade. ‘I was an angry-ass little kid,’ he recalled. ‘I was angry because my momma was gone … My little sister dead … Everything I got is gone, so I’m angry.’ Terrel came to read his anger and the violent behaviour it spawned as a verdict on himself. Beneath the easy smile others saw, he felt he was ‘just covering up [what’s inside] with that smile’: ‘I been fucking up the community for years. How the fuck am I good?’

In sum, many we spoke to had come to see themselves not simply as people who had done bad things, but as bad people. By their own accounts, accepting violence as part of who they were made their future involvement in violence more likely.

Violence alters how people experience the world and read everyday encounters. These patterns are neither irrational nor pathological. They are adaptations to real danger, where quick responses can save a life. But carried into the wrong situation, the same shortcuts can be overgeneralised in ways that cause grave harm.

While the stakes of these cognitive patterns are exceptional, the mental machinery underpinning them is not. Say you’re driving and another car cuts you off. Before you’ve even thought about it, your mind has supplied a reason: This driver is reckless and has no regard for anyone else on the road. The interpretation arrives in a split second, built more out of your irritation than anything you know about the driver. Maybe she’s racing to a hospital for an emergency. The writer David Foster Wallace described such a scene in his commencement speech, ‘This Is Water’ (2005). His point was hopeful: we are free to choose how we read such a moment. The automatic, egocentric perspective is never the only one available.

Nuke’s mind did the same when a stranger held his gaze too long. The look may have meant nothing, yet he imagined a motive and a threat, drawn from his life, as most of us do, rather than anything the stranger had done. Nuke is working with the same machinery as the rest of us. What that machinery was trained on is different, and so is the price of getting it wrong. For the driver, a misreading ends in a muttered curse or a blown horn; for Nuke, it could end a life. As Nuke admitted: ‘I know what comes with it. It’s either death or jail.’

We tend to imagine that we take in the world and then respond to what we find. In fact, the mind guides what we see, filling gaps with expectations built from experience. The journalist Walter Lippmann in 1922 called these expectations ‘the pictures in our heads’ and explained that it is the pictures we respond to, not some objective environmental stimuli. Psychologists and sociologists call these shortcuts frames and scripts. Frames answer, in a fraction of a second, the question under every social encounter: What is going on here? Scripts suggest what to do next. Together they help us move through our days without deliberating over each interaction. Frames and scripts are tools that make daily life possible.
The vigilance that keeps someone alive at one point can generate danger at another

Among the men we spoke with, these shortcuts took their shape from a world that taught a brutal lesson early: people are dangerous, and hesitation can get you hurt. The lesson came from somewhere. The sociologist Elijah Anderson in 1994 called it the ‘code of the streets’. Where safety is not a given, a reputation for violence becomes the protection people can supply themselves. The frame comes first: this is a threat. The script that follows, I have to fight back, is learned from experience and reinforced by others.

But a shortcut is only as good as it is accurate. Threat-oriented frames and scripts may be adaptive in the specific situations that produced them, but the same reading carried into an uncertain moment can be destructive and self-defeating. The vigilance that keeps someone alive at one point can generate danger at another, converting an ambiguous situation into a hostile one and producing the very conflict it anticipated. The mind continues to guard against a world that is, in part, no longer there.

Of course, the milieu that trained these frames and scripts has not entirely disappeared for most. Recall that young men in these neighbourhoods faced a greater risk of being killed than a soldier deployed to Iraq or Afghanistan. A soldier, though, eventually returns home; these men have no such separation. What they must learn is more complex: how to hold on to vigilance without letting it dictate their reactions in the wrong place or at the wrong moment. The problem is not the impulse to fight back itself, but being unable to distinguish situations that call for it from those that don’t.

The idea that changing how we see can change how we respond is ancient. In the 2nd century, Epictetus said: ‘Men are disturbed not by things, but by the views which they take of them.’ What is unusual is its application. Offering the opportunity to reframe a situation, as a serious answer to lethal violence, to a 26-year-old sitting in his room with a loaded clip is a novel proposition. It begins from an assumption too rarely extended to men like King with a history of violence: that despite what he has been through, his inner life is not fixed.

READI offered men a chance to discipline their inner worlds. The 18-month intervention paired a part-time job with cognitive behavioural sessions, held three to five mornings a week, that participants called ‘CAD’ (Control-Alt-Delete, the keystroke that reboots a computer). The lessons taught participants how to slow down to reconsider an automatic reaction and widen the range of responses in a tense moment. They learned that they did not have to be ruled by their first feeling or thought. In doing so, they began to loosen the identity that violence had formed

A randomised controlled trial of READI estimated that participants were arrested for shootings and homicides 65 per cent less often than comparable men who were not offered the programme. Findings from a related programme point in the same direction. Becoming a Man, a school-based programme run in Chicago by the nonprofit organisation Youth Guidance, cut violent-crime arrests among high-school-age participants by nearly half. Our interviews complement these trials by showing what the changes these programmes brought felt like from the inside.
What seemed to be a threat from the man across the street might be coming from somewhere much older

The first thing the men learned was to question their reading of a situation. In one CAD session, the group was given a scenario: somebody walks past and calls you a name. What do you do? For TY, 20, who had spent his adolescence surviving, the old answer would have arrived without thought. Instead, he worked through it. ‘I ain’t got no right to cause hurt to another person [if] this person ain’t do nothing to me,’ he said. ‘He probably having a bad day. He probably just got into it with his wife. You don’t know what’s wrong.’ Such exercises helped participants practise reframing a situation more charitably.

Questioning a reading also meant learning that a feeling of threat was not always about what was happening in the present; sometimes, it was a reaction to events in the past. The men practised noticing what fear was doing in their bodies, such as a racing pulse, tightened fists, pressure in the chest, and learning to treat those sensations as signals to investigate rather than signs of objective threats. Larry, 31, described it as learning to check in with his body: ‘Far as articulating the things that’s going on inside of my body and how I’m feeling, that’s what I’m really learning.’ What seemed to be a threat from the man across the street might, at times, be coming from somewhere much older.

Second, they learned to see more than one possible response to feeling threatened. Kobe described his old reflex as follows: ‘If you said something, I was going to touch you or tap you or get on your ass.’ Now, Kobe said: ‘I think before I act.’ Recalling a role-play in which he was bumped outside a store, he laid out what he could now see: ‘I could whoop one of they ass and one of them could shoot me… or I could just walk away. Or I could ask him, did he mean to do it?’ Three options emerged where there had previously been one.

To help them remember they had options in the moment, the men developed mantras simple enough to recall under pressure. Keith, 24, learned to: ‘Take 10 deep breaths, pace back and forth, and you might see things differently.’ Tune, 30, used: ‘It only takes three seconds to ruin your life.’ Larry, in a fight with his son’s mother, told himself: ‘It’s just words.’

Finally, participants learned to distinguish what they had done from who they were. Jaysean, 22, had taken the bad things he had done as proof that he was a bad person. Abandoned by kin while still a boy, he had sought out older robbers to teach him how to survive. He said: ‘A lot of things that I did bad, I did it for survival. Cause I didn’t really know no other way to get no money.’ Jaysean explained: ‘I was looking for the wrong help. I didn’t know no better. You a product of your environment to a certain extent.’ The reframing allowed him to imagine a self no longer defined by his past: ‘I’m a good person within… I’m still falling down but I’m picking myself back up.’ What Jaysean had once believed was a sign of his character, he could now see as a result of surviving tough circumstances.

Terrel reached the same realisation by naming the trauma he had long carried. ‘I never got through my first trauma,’ he said of his sister’s death; in the years since, he had lost a brother, a cousin, a nephew and friend after friend. ‘That shit just fucked me up to this day. I’m suffering with PTSD bad.’ Understanding his behaviour as a response to those losses, rather than as proof of who he was, made change imaginable. As Terrel said: ‘If you don’t deal with it… you can bring that baggage into your adult life.’ Naming the ways in which his past spilled into the present through his PTSD allowed Terrel to challenge his own narrative about himself and begin to heal.

These are ancient skills. READI’s contribution was not inventing them but building a place where men could practise them. These changes required certain conditions. READI’s wages gave the men enough stability to keep returning, and staff created a space safe enough for them to lower their guard, even around those participants they previously considered rivals. The pay check may have been what initially brought them in, but it was not how they ultimately understood the programme. In fact, 70 per cent described READI primarily as an opportunity for personal growth rather than just a job, and they spoke at length about how it reshaped their closest relationships, their daily habits, even their sense of who they were.

Which brings us back to King, in his room, with the clip full. Despite his initial instincts, he did not join his cousin to retaliate. He put the gun down and stayed put. ‘So I got high and I sat right there and just calmed myself down,’ he told us. ‘I shed a couple of tears for my boy and said: “Everything going to be all right.”’ It was the very mantra he had been practising in READI. King’s grief had not abated. What had changed was that revenge no longer felt inevitable. ‘Why I go try to waste my life for nothing?’ he asked. ‘That’s not me no more.’ In the space between feeling and action, King could see another response.

King did not arrive at that response alone. For months, he had practised slowing down and questioning his first reaction with other men. READI did not make the danger around him less real, nor did it ask him to abandon the vigilance that had sometimes kept him alive. Rather, it helped him more clearly discern the moments it threatened to reproduce the very violence he feared.

This is where I part with Wallace. He was right that we can choose how to read a situation, but he underestimated what such a choice requires. For the men we interviewed, seeing differently was not just a private act of will performed alone in traffic. It was something they practised repeatedly with others, under conditions of safety, enough time and skilled support.
‘I didn’t know that if you yelled at me, I was gonna break down. But now I [see]: it’s not you, it’s a past trigger’

I have seen the same skills taught in a classroom, on a corner by an outreach worker, and in a boxing gym in the Chicago neighbourhood of North Lawndale, where the former gang member Derek Brown* has been running a programme called Boxing Out Negativity since 2009. He teaches boys to box and, alongside it, to sit still and breathe, to notice what their bodies are doing before a fight and after one, to name what they are feeling and to wait. The boys come to Derek’s gym to learn how to fight. They are also learning how to handle the moments before a fight starts, which is the harder lesson and the one they need more often in life.

These skills are also useful to people who meet others in moments of crises. LaToya Baines* manages victim advocates on Chicago’s West Side who spend their days supporting people through the worst moments of their lives, and who bring their own histories to that work. She learned the same techniques through training and now teaches them to her staff. ‘Once you learn, you’re able to identify those triggers. I didn’t know that if you yelled at me, I was gonna break down. But now I’m able to [see]: it’s not you, it’s a past trigger. I just stepped back into the past, for something else that happened to me that has nothing to do with you.’ Chicago police officers are being taught to do the same thing, through a programme called Situational Decision-Making. Officers who went through it used less force and made fewer discretionary arrests.

None of this is particular to places where violence is the problem. When my husband and I started having conversations about merging our finances, I would respond by shutting down and becoming frustrated. He studies financial decision-making for a living, and talking about money was second-nature to him. For me it was physically painful. My chest would tighten, and I would go quiet, get anxious or find a reason to end the conversation.

It took me a long time to understand why. In the family in which I grew up, we didn’t talk about money. When we had it, nobody mentioned it. Then we lost our house, my parents divorced, and money was a more frequently discussed issue. It wasn’t until years later, while having conversations about finances with my husband that stirred negative responses in me, that I recognised how I automatically logged a conversation about money as the beginning of something going wrong. With help from a cognitive behavioural therapist and my very patient husband, I learned what the men in READI learned: to notice a reactive feeling in my body, to have compassion for myself about where it came from, and to recognise when it no longer served me.

Violence teaches the mind what to expect and how to answer. Because these are learned habits, they can be remade. A mind formed amid violence is not fixed by it. But few people revise their habits of mind on their own, sitting in traffic and deciding to see things differently. With proper training, people can learn to question their first reading of a situation, to see more than one response available to them, and to stop taking what they have done as proof of who they are. They learn, in other words, that their pasts need not define their present. The capacity is ordinary. What is not is the safety and ongoing support it takes to use it.

A young woman pulled into the run-up to a political massacre slides from unwilling witness to accomplice in “Once Upon a Time in the Philippines,” the debut feature from E del Mundo inspired by the 2009 Maguindanao massacre.
The project is part of the Asian Project Market, which runs within the Busan International Film Festival’s Asian Contents & Film Market (ACFM).

Set in an invented locale that nods to the country’s south, the film centers on Sam, a 19-year-old who works at a gas station and gets caught up in killings by the private army of a political clan. In the aftermath, she hunts for her boyfriend, now missing and possibly a participant in the slaughter, and finds that one institution after another is bound up in the same apparatus of violence.

In 2009, armed men stopped a convoy of civilians, relatives, lawyers and journalists heading to submit election filings in Maguindanao and killed 58 people, at least 32 of them journalists and media workers. The producers note that it is widely considered the deadliest single attack on journalists on record.

Del Mundo was raised under the weight of an event she says the Philippines has never truly come to terms with. “I came to believe that atrocities of this magnitude are rarely the work of a single monster. They are made possible by a multitude of people who obey, participate, remain silent, or simply stop asking questions,” she says. “That conviction transformed the film into something closer to a forensic examination of myself within my own society.”

She is drawn to the fragility of a woman’s mind inside a stifling life shaped by men, and the steady acceptance of the violence built into it. Del Mundo calls the film “a coming-of-age story swallowed whole by the political reality of the Philippines,” and uses Sam, though fictional, as her route into a collective trauma. “I hope audiences leave with the recognition that we belong to something larger than ourselves, and that something larger also lives within us, the good, the bad, and the ugly of it all,” she says.

The film is produced by Kyle Nieva and Gian Carlo Librojo of the Philippines’ Screen Asia with Pamela Reyes, in co-production with France’s Piano Sano Films and Norway’s DUOfilm. Co-producers are Idris Lettifi, Marie Fuglestein Lægreid, Linda Bolstad Strønen and Ingrid Lill Høgtun. Screen Asia also produced del Mundo’s VR film “Yellowfin,” which premiered at Cannes.

Nieva says the earlier collaboration gave the producers strong faith in del Mundo’s vision, and that she approaches political violence through one young woman’s experience rather than spectacle. For Librojo, a broadcast journalist, the project carries a personal weight. “The massacre cannot be treated only as a closed chapter in history. It reveals structures of political power, fear, and impunity that continue to shape Philippine society,” Librojo says.

The project has been through Cannes’ Cinéfondation L’Atelier and Producers Network, the Venice Gap-Financing Market, Locarno Open Doors, where it won a development award and a Sørfond award, TorinoFilmLab, where it took the FOCAL Resource Award, and the Singapore International Film Festival’s Southeast Asian Film Lab. It has backing from the CNC and Institut français’ Aide aux cinémas du monde, the Norwegian Film Institute’s Sørfond, Visions Sud Est and Purin Pictures.

Now in advanced financing after years of development, the team is using Busan to close the remaining gap and meet partners to take the film into production. “After such a long development journey, we hope Busan can be the final bridge between development and production,” Nieva says.

We know all about how things exist in the three dimensions of length, width, and height. Physicists often talk about time as a fourth dimension, but what if there were a fourth spatial dimension — another direction entirely? How on earth would we picture that?

Mathematicians use topology to visualize abstract spaces in higher dimensions. Maggie Miller at the University of Texas at Austin explores what happens when knots encounter an extra dimension. Familiar tangled loops behave in unexpectedly complex and counterintuitive ways in 4D: Knots can always come undone, while ordinary surfaces like spheres can — surprisingly — become knotted in ways that can’t be undone.

In this episode, Miller explains to co-host Janna Levin why 4D is the lowest dimension that mathematicians still don’t fully understand, how she and her collaborators resolved a question about knotted surfaces first posed by mathematician Charles Livingston in 1982, and how her interest in art has helped her develop the visual techniques she uses to picture 4D spaces.

LEVIN: With these four-dimensional spaces and your intuition faltering, what are the kinds of questions that you’re asking? What are the hypotheses that you’re really pursuing?

If I took a piece of string… Wait, I actually, I have a string. MILLER: Well, less like a ribbon and more like a balloon. So I wanna have an object that doesn’t have any edges. But there’s also more complicated surfaces. So a balloon is a sphere or a 2-sphere. It’s very common to say the dimension of the space.

It’s two-dimensional because if I’m standing on a balloon, then I can go forward, backward, left, right on the balloon, but if I try to go up, I’ll leave the balloon. Maybe instead of a balloon, I should say the surface of the Earth, another example of a two-dimensional sphere. If I go up into space, then I leave the surface of the Earth, so it’s only two-dimensional.

But there are more spaces, like for example, a torus, which is the two-dimensional space that I would get if an asteroid hit the Earth and drilled straight through. So there’s a hole in it now. It’s the surface of that. I think it’d be more normal to say it’s the surface of a bagel or a donut. And then there’s more spaces that I could get if I have more holes.

LEVIN: And so that way you make more and more complicated spaces far beyond the simplicity of the smooth, compact, connected three-dimensional sphere. You make these very complicated spaces with handles and holes and kind of an origami.

Scientists may have found a shortcut to fusion energy
Scientists have uncovered a potentially far more efficient path to fusion ignition that could bring the dream of practical fusion energy closer to reality.

- Princeton Plasma Physics Laboratory may have found a dramatically more efficient route to fusion energy by reversing the traditional approach: heating plasma first, then increasing its density. Their calculations could help future reactors reach self-sustaining fusion with far less energy while avoiding hidden problems that make ignition harder.

Scientists at the U.S.Department of Energy's (DOE) Princeton Plasma Physics Laboratory (PPPL) have identified a potentially much more efficient way to achieve fusion ignition, a major milestone in the pursuit of practical fusion energy. Their calculations suggest that changing the order in which plasma is heated and compressed could dramatically reduce the energy needed to reach a self-sustaining fusion reaction.

For more than seven decades, fusion researchers have relied on a mathematical rule to determine whether plasma can remain sufficiently hot and dense, for a long enough period, to sustain fusion without additional external heating. Known as the Lawson criterion, this equation defines the conditions required for ignition. However, it does not explain the most efficient way to achieve them.

Now, PPPL physicists Luis Delgado-Aparicio, Masayuki Ono, and Jonathan Menard have developed a more comprehensive version of the criterion. By incorporating four additional factors that influence fusion performance, they have mapped a promising route to ignition that could require substantially less energy than alternative approaches.
Their findings were published in the journal Physical Review Letters.

The research focuses on plasma, often called the fourth state of matter. Plasma forms when a gas becomes so energetic that its particles carry electrical charges. In fusion reactors, this extremely hot material contains the atomic nuclei that researchers hope to combine, releasing energy through nuclear fusion.

The ultimate goal is to produce a burning plasma, in which fusion reactions generate enough heat to sustain the process without continued external heating. Reaching this state efficiently remains one of the most important challenges in fusion energy research.
Scientists Find a Shortcut to Fusion Ignition
Delgado-Aparicio compares the discovery to finding a more efficient route through a mountain range.
Imagine that the energy requirements for fusion ignition form a landscape dominated by a towering mountain. The destination lies on the other side, but there are several possible routes to reach it.

Many proposed fusion strategies effectively attempt to climb directly over the mountain. They begin by increasing the density of the plasma and then supplying the enormous amount of heat needed to reach ignition.

The new calculations suggest that a different sequence could be considerably more efficient. Instead of increasing density first, researchers could heat the plasma before making it denser. This alternative route avoids the highest energy requirements while still reaching the desired conditions.

"A lot of companies want to climb the mountain head-on and spend enormous energy to get there," Delgado-Aparicio said. "Go around the peak instead. You reach the same place in a much smarter way, and you use far less energy."
The Hidden Mountain Pass in Fusion Physics
The researchers identified a particularly important region of this mathematical landscape called the Cordey saddle.

In geographical terms, a saddle is a low passage between higher elevations. In fusion physics, the Cordey saddle represents a relatively accessible point along the boundary separating plasma that still needs outside heating from plasma capable of sustaining its own fusion reactions.
To evaluate different routes, the scientists used a measurement called Q, which compares the power produced by fusion reactions with the external heating power supplied to the plasma.
For example, a Q value of 5 means the fusion reactions produce five times as much power as the external heating system delivers.

In an idealized plasma containing only pure fusion fuel, the Cordey saddle occurs at approximately Q = 5. However, actual fusion systems are much more complicated. Contaminants within the plasma and extremely strong magnetic fields can shift the location of this passage, increasing the Q value needed to reach it.
Understanding how these conditions change is essential for determining whether a proposed fusion reactor can realistically achieve ignition.
A More Realistic Roadmap for Future Fusion Reactors
The findings could influence the design of two major types of magnetic fusion devices: tokamaks and stellarators.

Both approaches use powerful magnetic fields to confine plasma while it is heated to the extraordinary temperatures needed for fusion. Tokamaks, which have a characteristic doughnut shape, are among the leading technologies being investigated for future fusion power plants.

Research institutions and private companies are pursuing several different ways to generate electricity from fusion and eventually deliver that power to the electrical grid. Identifying an efficient route to ignition could help engineers design more practical systems while avoiding costly mistakes.

For PPPL, this work is part of a broader effort to address the scientific and technological challenges that must be overcome before commercial fusion power becomes possible, including the development of future fusion pilot plants.
One of the study's major advances is that it evaluates several important physical processes together rather than examining them separately, as much previous research has done.
The researchers incorporated four additional factors that can influence whether a plasma reaches and maintains ignition:
- Helium ash buildup: Fusion reactions produce helium as a byproduct. As this spent fuel accumulates, it can dilute the remaining fusion fuel and reduce performance.
- Plasma contamination: Light and heavy impurities can enter the plasma from materials lining the inside of the reactor, interfering with fusion conditions.
- Synchrotron radiation: Electrons traveling through magnetic fields emit radiation, carrying energy away from the plasma.
- Heat loss: Energy continuously escapes from the plasma, and these losses can become greater as its temperature rises.
Accounting for these effects produces a more realistic picture of the conditions future reactors must achieve.
"When you leave these effects out, you say the design will work fine," Ono said. "When you put them in, the picture changes, and it becomes quite important."
According to Ono, the goal is to establish a more reliable, widely applicable model that scientists can use to evaluate fusion reactor designs before construction begins.

Treating the Lawson criterion as a single unchanging threshold overlooks physical processes that can substantially alter the requirements for ignition. Including those effects early in the design process could prevent expensive problems later.
"Fusion experiments cost a great deal of money, and you do not want to make mistakes you could have caught beforehand," he said.
Tiny Amounts of Tungsten Could Make Fusion Much Harder
One particularly striking finding concerns tungsten, an extremely heat-resistant metal selected for the interior walls of more than a dozen next-generation fusion machines.

Tungsten is attractive because fusion reactors must withstand conditions involving plasma temperatures greater than those found at the center of the sun. However, the material also presents a significant challenge if even tiny quantities enter the plasma.
The team's calculations show that tungsten contamination at a concentration of just one part in 10,000 can approximately double the pressure required to achieve fusion ignition.
That is a substantial increase caused by an exceptionally small amount of material.

The calculations were initially developed in two dimensions. When the researchers extended their analysis to three dimensions, they found that the pressure needed for ignition could exceed the limits at which the plasma remains stable.
This suggests that seemingly minor contamination could have major consequences for the feasibility of certain fusion reactor designs.
How Energy Losses Could Help Stabilize Fusion
Surprisingly, some of the processes that make ignition more difficult may also help fusion reactors operate more safely and consistently.

Scientists have long investigated the possibility of thermal "runaway" instability. This occurs when heat from fusion reactions increases the reaction rate, producing still more heat and potentially creating a self-reinforcing cycle.
The researchers found that energy losses within the plasma can naturally counteract this effect.

Although those losses increase the difficulty of reaching ignition, they also provide a balancing influence that could allow a burning plasma to maintain a stable operating state without constant adjustments.
This balance could be valuable for future reactor designs.
(Unlike a fission power plant, a fusion system holds only seconds of fuel at a time, so losing control means the plasma cools and the burn stops rather than anything worse.)
Liquid Lithium and Advanced Fuel Could Improve Fusion Efficiency
The study also identifies technologies that might help overcome some of the obstacles revealed by the calculations.
One possibility involves coating the inside of fusion reactors with liquid lithium, a technique PPPL researchers have investigated for years.
These coatings could help prevent tungsten from entering the plasma while reducing heat losses, making it easier to maintain the extreme conditions necessary for fusion.
Another promising approach uses spin-polarized fuel. This involves preparing the atomic nuclei so that their spins are aligned before fusion occurs, which can increase the fusion reaction rate.
Together, these strategies could improve the performance of future reactors and make the path to ignition more achievable.
What Comes Next for the New Fusion Strategy?
Despite the promising findings, the proposed heat-first approach has not yet been demonstrated experimentally.

The research is theoretical and relies on mathematical calculations rather than direct measurements. Existing fusion experiments have not reached the temperatures associated with the Cordey saddle, preventing scientists from testing the predicted route under those conditions.

The PPPL team plans to investigate the approach further through digital experiments, using computer-based simulations to explore whether heating plasma before increasing its density can deliver the expected advantages.

If future studies confirm the calculations, the findings could provide an important foundation for designing more efficient fusion systems and help researchers make better decisions about reactor construction.
"While more study is needed, we are excited by these results, and they suggest a clear path forward for future research in this area," said Menard.

Christa Pike discharged from the hospital and back in prison

Christa Pike was released from a local hospital and is back in prison, at the Debra K. Johnson Rehabilitation Center in Tennessee, her attorneys Luke Ihnen, Randy Spivey, Stephen Ferrell and Kelly Gleason said in a statement on Saturday.
"She is grateful to the first responders and her medical team for their care in these extraordinary circumstances," the attorneys said.
They also said Pike is receiving medical care at the prison and they are tracking her recovery.
Pike had been hospitalized for several days after her botched execution last month, in which she received and survived two doses of the sedative pentobarbital.

NPR reported on the Sept. 30 execution attempt, in which Pike was strapped to a gurney and administered the barbiturate that is normally used in the U.S. executions. Shortly after the first dose was administered, Pike said her arm was burning and asked whether it was supposed to feel that way. She then said, "Please try up on my shoulder higher."

Spivey, who witnessed the execution attempt, previously told NPR that after a second dose Pike became unconscious but continued breathing and making choking sounds. "It "went on for so long," he said. He has called Pike "a survivor."
Judge I'Ashea Myles of the Davidson County Chancery Court in Nashville ordered the prison officials to preserve all evidence, such as messages, connected to Pike's failed execution.

Pike was on death row for a murder she committed when she was 18 years old. She and her boyfriend, Tadaryl Shipp, in 1995, tortured and killed 19-year-old Colleen Slemmer, a fellow classmate in the Knoxville Job Corps. Shipp received life in prison without parole for his part in the murder.
NPR's Scott Neuman contributed to this report.

Less than two months ago, Oregon was considered a favorite to win the national championship. It put together one of the most expensive rosters in the country, and Dante Moore turned down the possibility of being a top-10 NFL Draft pick to return for one more College Football Playoff run.
Following a 17-15 loss to No. 21 UCLA, the Ducks have a good case as the most disappointing team in the country, and their margin for error is gone.

After Oregon overcame the loss of Moore to beat USC on the road in Week 4, it seemed like the Ducks were on the path back to contention. They got an open date to prepare backup quarterback Dylan Raiola before hosting the Bruins and were comfortable favorites in Autzen Stadium.
Then the game started, and what ensued was a disaster of epic proportions for Oregon.

Raiola was 6-of-19 with 43 yards and two interceptions before getting benched in the second half. On the ground, Oregon averaged just 2.7 yards per carry. It converted one of 12 third-down attempts. The Ducks turned the ball over seven times.

Despite all that, Oregon had a chance to tie the game on a two-point conversion with just over two minutes remaining. After a facemask penalty against UCLA, the Ducks needed one yard. Their vaunted offensive line got knocked back, and Jordon Davison got stuffed for no gain.

The circumstances weren't ideal for Oregon with Moore out, but it had the best backup quarterback in the nation, at least on paper. Besides, the Bruins didn't even play the full game with their starting quarterback because Nico Iamaleava exited the contest with an injury of his own and was replaced by Ty Dieffenbach.

With two losses and three weeks until Halloween, the Ducks and their $40 million roster are officially out of mulligans despite boasting one of the most expensive rosters in college football. If they want any chance at reaching the College Football Playoff, they'll have to go undefeated the rest of the way, and they have a date with Ohio State in Columbus on Nov. 7.
Then again, no game is a layup based on how disappointing Oregon has been through the first six weeks of the season.
After Raiola took over for the injured Moore against USC, it looked as though his decision to accept a backup role in Eugene would benefit both parties greatly.

Raiola completed 75% of his passes for 289 yards and two touchdowns in just over two quarters of work. With an open date to prepare for UCLA, Oregon had to feel good about its quarterback situation, even with Moore unavailable due to a concussion.

Instead, some of the same issues that plagued Raiola at Nebraska popped up against the Bruins. Raiola was careless with the ball and tried to do too much on several plays. The result was two interceptions and a fumble while Raiola completed less than 33% of his attempts.
How did an experienced quarterback like Raiola look so unprepared at home? That's a question Dan Lanning will have to answer in the wake of this devastating loss.

At least there will be no more rumblings of a quarterback controversy when Moore returns, which the Ducks hope is next week. If Moore misses a second straight game next week, will Lanning put his team's fate in the hands of Brock Thomas, a senior and former three-star recruit?
No one saw Oregon sitting at 3-2 on Oct. 10. There was too much talent on the roster for anyone to forecast losses to Oklahoma State and UCLA prior to Week 1.

If the Ducks are going to accomplish their goal of reaching the College Football Playoff, they need to go 7-0 the rest of the season. That's a tall task for a team that has yet to show any kind of consistency in 2026, but the good news is that the upcoming schedule is manageable.

Oregon gets Nebraska next week, and the Cornhuskers are coming off a soul-crushing loss of their own. After that, Oregon gets Northwestern and Illinois, which should be wins even if the team isn't at its best.

If Moore comes back healthy and looks like himself, Oregon has enough firepower to overwhelm most of the opponents remaining on its schedule. Michigan hasn't been able to move the football on offense, and Washington is 3-3 after getting hammered by Iowa.

That means the season likely comes down to the road game against Ohio State on Nov. 7. Thus far, the Ducks have shown nothing to indicate they're capable of beating the Buckeyes on the road, but the talent is on the roster, at least in theory.

He calls for building a more transparent system where models can be contained, observed, and leaves behind “tamper-proof human readable evidence.”
Satya Nadella says we should assume all AI models are ‘compromised’
Microsoft’s CEO calls for putting an ‘emergency brake’ on AI.

Many of his recommendations align with what we’ve heard from others in the industry: timely incident disclosure, independent audits, verifiable data, and containment. It’s on that last point that he appears to go slightly farther than some others in the field, saying:

Astronomers have obtained the most detailed image to date of the Pa 30 nebula, the remnants of a supernova famous for having likely been observed and documented from Earth during the Middle Ages. Now, the new photograph reveals structures that had long gone unnoticed.

Previous images of the explosion’s remnants had also captured a sphere of long, filament-like strands of matter that collectively resemble fireworks or a dandelion. The new observations, made with the Gemini North telescope in Hawaii, revealed about 10 times more structures than any previous glimpses of the supernova remnant. With this resolution, researchers can now see that these filaments are not continuous as they had previously appeared. Instead, they’re shaped more like beads on a string, made up of pearl-like knots of gas of relatively uniform size.

These “cosmic pearls” are, in fact, enormous. According to the study published in The Astrophysical Journal, each bead measures about four light-days in diameter. “The planetary region of our solar system could fit in each knot about 10 times with room to spare,” Ilaria Caiazzo, a coauthor of the study, said in a press release. “The knots are quite strikingly uniform. We are excited to try to model them.”

How exactly the pearls formed is not yet entirely clear, though it’s assumed they are concentrations of material ejected during the explosion. What’s strange, however, is their regularity. In the aftermath of a supernova, astronomers expected to find much more oddly shaped accumulations, but the knots are similar in size and appear aligned along the filaments. This peculiar order is a new feature that could help researchers gain a deeper understanding of stellar death.

The Pa 30 nebula is also particularly unusual because the central star isn’t exactly dead. Instead, it’s considered a “zombie star.” Typically, a thermonuclear supernova is the violent death of a star, which is completely destroyed in the explosion. But in rare cases, part of the star may survive, and scientists do not yet fully understand how or why this happens. The unusual structures of Pa 30 could help astronomers reconstruct more precisely how these kinds of detonations occur and how zombie stars can live on afterward.

All of this has been discovered because scientists seem to have a bit of a crush on Pa 30. Few astronomical structures connect modern observation so directly with human accounts from more than eight centuries ago. The nebula matches the records left by Chinese and Japanese astronomers in 1181, who described the appearance of a new star in the sky that remained visible for several months. At the time, it was impossible to know that they were witnessing the aftermath of a massive stellar explosion. Centuries later, scientists linked that event to the supernova that gave rise to Pa 30.

The U.S. Army awarded $43 million to defense company Kaizen Laboratories to create application software for highly sensitive military material.

The $49 million Enterprise Agreement Indefinite Delivery, Indefinite Quantity contract, or IDIQ, specifically focuses on mission and enterprise applications, staff workflows, records and “reporting that sit above the Army’s systems of record,” a Kaizen release said.

“The Army is changing how it acquires software because missions cannot wait through years of bespoke implementation,” said Nikhil Reddy, co-founder and CEO of Kaizen Labs. “This agreement provides Army organizations a more direct path to the applications essential to their critical operations.”

Though the amount could increase based on demand, the remaining $6 million in the contract could be used to fund software for military readiness, personnel management, installations, logistics or operations, Reddy told Military Times.
For instance, a service member might use a Defense Department web portal under the Morale, Welfare and Recreation program to book lodging for an event.

That reservation platform includes components like data and scheduling mechanisms. But that platform that allows a service member or the Defense Department to manage a particular reservation likely hosts numerous digital properties that apply to other services and platforms soldiers use, Reddy said.

If, hypothetically, the military wanted Kaizen to revamp case management portals, the company could perform that task while addressing multiple areas of need by supplying new application software for multiple portals across the military.
Kaizen is no stranger to helping the Defense Department streamline important processes.
In August, the company built the online counter-unmanned aerial system marketplace that allows verified DoD buyers to purchase autonomous systems.

Kaizen developed the marketplace with Joint Interagency Task Force 401, which spearheads efforts to bridge the gap between government agencies and defense tech companies pushing counter-drone technology.
The biggest problem with fielding technologies is procurement, Reddy told Military Times.
Legal frameworks, contract vehicles and purchasing agreements can take forever at the pace and scale that the Pentagon needs, he said.
So, Kaizen built the Airbnb equivalent for counter-UAS systems, Reddy said.
American companies can now log onto the marketplace, post products and receive procurement contracts from interested DoD-affiliated parties.
Under the $49 IDIQ, the Army and Kaizen’s framework agreement allows the service to order different products now and in the future.
Riley Ceder is a Navy reporter at Military Times, where he covers issues directly affecting service members and their families, as well as breaking news.

ESA astronaut Sophie Adenot has arrived back in Europe, landing in Cologne, Germany, following her return to Earth with Crew-12 after 237 days, nearly eight months, aboard the International Space Station for her εpsilon mission.

After splashdown on 8 October at 15:34 GMT/17:34 CEST and initial medical checks aboard the recovery vessel, Sophie and her crewmates travelled to shore by helicopter before boarding a NASA plane at the nearest airport. They were flown together to Ellington Field in Houston for initial post-flight activities.

On 9 October Sophie boarded a French Air and Space Force Airbus A330 MRTT Phénix bound for ESA’s European Astronaut Centre (EAC) in Cologne, Germany. She landed at 04:21 GMT / 06:21 CEST on 10 October and was warmly welcomed on the apron by family, friends, colleagues, journalists and representatives from ESA Member States.

“We are delighted to welcome back our ESA astronaut Sophie Adenot who embodied our values through her successful mission,” says Josef Aschbacher, ESA’s Director General. “The inspiration that Sophie has provided with her mission matters a great deal as we enter into such a decisive moment for Europe. Human spaceflight and exploration remain at the centre of our attention as we prepare for the Intermediate Ministerial Council Meeting in Rome in December. Our ambition is clear: Europe must secure a role in exploration commensurate with its political and economic weight.”

Sophie will spend the next two to three weeks adjusting to Earth’s gravity and undergoing data collections at :envihab, a German Aerospace Center (DLR) facility located next to EAC. DLR teams work closely with ESA, providing operational, medical and scientific expertise to support astronauts’ return, recovery and readaptation to life on Earth. Sophie will then continue her rehabilitation and follow-up activities with the EAC training team.

Sophie spent a total of 237 days, 5 hours and 18 minutes in space after being launched on 13 February 2026 from Cape Canaveral Space Force Station in Florida, USA. The εpsilon mission set a new European record for the longest single spaceflight, exceeding by more than 35 days the previous record held by ESA astronaut Luca Parmitano for his Beyond mission. Crew-12 is also the longest SpaceX Dragon mission to date, surpassing the previous record of 235 days set by Crew-8.

Sophie is the second European woman, after ESA astronaut Samantha Cristoforetti, and the first French woman to conduct an Extra Vehicular Activity (EVA), or spacewalk. Sophie completed three spacewalks in 14 days, spending a total of 19 hours and 42 minutes working outside the Station. Throughout εpsilon, Sophie carried out a wide range of European experiments spanning fields from health research to materials science, biology, fluid physics, radiation physics and fundamental science.

Over the course of Expedition 74 and 75, Sophie worked on experiments and payloads for International Space Station partners, contributing to the international research programme carried out aboard the orbiting laboratory.

Sophie also spent around 218 hours working on 35 European payloads, and about 25 hours on ESA systems maintenance or upgrades in Columbus, Europe’s microgravity research facility in orbit. She completed all the εpsilon-specific experiments proposed by the French space agency CNES, and all ESA experiments that were assigned to her.

“Sophie was the first of her class to be assigned to a mission, embarking on a fast-track journey she brilliantly completed. Her return now marks the successful completion of an outstanding mission aboard the International Space Station, says Daniel Neuenschwander, ESA Director of Human and Robotic Exploration. “During εpsilon, she has contributed to an ambitious programme of science, technology and exploration, while representing Europe in an international endeavour that depends on the commitment of thousands of people. Missions like εpsilon help build the knowledge, experience and inspiration we need as Europe pursues its ambitions for exploration and discovery. We are immensely proud to welcome her back to Europe and grateful to all the teams and partners who supported her throughout this journey.”

During her free time, Sophie took more than 1,1 million social media followers along on the εpsilon adventure, sharing insights into the science experiments she worked on and life aboard the Station, as well as views of Earth from orbit and her Sunday Morning Science series, which took advantage of microgravity to demonstrate scientific concepts. Sophie’s social media content during εpsilon generated more than 403 million views.

Sophie also reached and inspired more than 290 000 students through the CNES educational experiment Chloriss conducted in about 4000 schools, ESA’s AstroPi challenge, the International Space Station’s amateur radio programme ARISS, and a poetry contest. She also took part in more than 40 live events with schools, museums, institutions and journalists around the world.

True to the meaning behind εpsilon, Sophie’s contribution was one of many that came together to make the mission possible. Behind εpsilon’s achievements was a collective effort involving ESA teams and centres across Europe, including EAC, the Columbus Control Centre (Col-CC) and the network of User Support and Operations Centres (USOCs), alongside national space agencies such as CNES and many partners.

Around 4,500 years ago, ancient Egyptians carved the Great Sphinx of Giza out of limestone in the Mokattam rock formation. Little did they know, the material they were digging through preserved something even more archaic: fossils of a long-extinct crocodile.

Researchers have identified a previously unknown species of gavial, a type of crocodilian with a long, thin snout, from a fossil originally found in the rock formation that the ancient Egyptians sculpted into the Sphinx and the Pyramids of Giza. The new identification corrects a previous erroneous classification, according to a study published October 7 in the journal Royal Society Open Science. It also sheds light on the fauna that existed in what’s now Egypt well before human-made monuments appeared on the horizon.

In the 1920s, several fossilized remains, including a largely intact crocodile-like skull, emerged from the roughly 45-million-year-old Mokattam Formation at a site near Cairo. Because of the bones’ resemblance to those of Tomistoma schlegelii—a living gavial native to Indonesia and Malaysia—experts originally assigned them to the same Tomistoma genus. Until now, the well-preserved skull was the holotype, or name-bearing representative fossil, for the extinct T. cairense.

Thanks to modern paleontological techniques like micro-CT scanning, which allows researchers to see inside fossils without breaking them, the team behind the new work found many differences between Tomistoma and the Mokattam Formation crocs. Comparing measurements of the skull to those of modern and fossil gavials revealed that the roughly 18-inch-long noggin represented not just a new species, but a new genus as well.

They named it Herugavialis cairensis, drawing inspiration from the Egyptian god Heru, also known as Horus. Some Egyptian texts call the Sphinx “Horus of the Horizon.” The associations between the H. cairensis skull and the iconic Sphinx go beyond the material that yielded them. Both are missing the tips of their noses.
Did you know? The origin of the Sphinx’s name

The Egyptians did not refer to the great statue as the Sphinx. Rather, ancient Greeks started calling it that around 2,000 years after it was carved. They possibly did so because of its resemblance to their mythological sphinx, which had a lion’s body, a woman’s head and an eagle’s wings.

“We seek to connect Egypt’s deep natural history with its human history and the legacy of ancient Egyptian civilization,” study co-author Hesham Sallam, a paleontologist at Mansoura University in Egypt, tells the Washington Post’s Elijah Wolfson. “Crocodiles were part of the Nile ecosystem, which was central to Egyptian life, and they held an important place in ancient Egyptian belief and culture.”

Gavials, cousins of crocodiles and alligators, were once found throughout the world. The Mediterranean region was home to a diverse community of crocodilians, including gavials, during much of the last 50 million years, lead author Paul Burke, a paleontologist at the Swedish Museum of Natural History, says in a statement. In fact, H. cairensis would have shared its shallow marine habitat with at least two other gavial species. Today, however, there are only two surviving gavials: the previously mentioned T. schlegelii and Gavialis gangeticus, which is clinging to habitats in Nepal and northern India.
Both are endangered, Burke tells Science News’ Jake Buehler. “So we should know about them and their long history.”

Correcting the fossil species’ identification also “helps paint a better picture of what large predators were like in the region,” Alex Hastings, a paleontologist at the Science Museum of Minnesota who did not participate in the study, tells CNN’s Taylor Nicioli. “This expands the known variety of forms of these amazing long-snouted crocodilians across the Mediterranean in ancient times.”
In ancient times, travelers journeying to Egypt via the Mediterranean Sea often faced perilous conditions.

As the Greek historian Diodorus Siculus wrote in the first century B.C.E., a sandbank extended along much of the kingdom’s northern coast, “not discernible to any who approach without previous experience of these waters.” Sailors who “in their ignorance turn with gladness toward the shore suffer unexpected shipwreck when their vessels suddenly run aground,” Diodorus added, “and now and then, mariners who cannot see land in time because the country lies so low are cast ashore before they realize it.” The only “safe harbor” to be found on this stretch of coastline, the historian concluded, was Pharos, the island that housed the Lighthouse of Alexandria.

Standing an estimated 330 to 430 feet tall, the lighthouse was also known as Pharos, after the land where it stood. At the time of its creation in the third century B.C.E., it was one of the world’s tallest humanmade structures, second only to the Pyramids of Giza. The lighthouse dominated the landscape for more than a millennium, until the 14th century C.E., when it crumbled into the sea following a series of earthquakes.

Some 700 years later, few traces of the lighthouse remain. But excavations on the neighboring island of Antirhodos, the site of an ancient palace that hosted the likes of Mark Antony and Cleopatra, have revealed a rare artifact linked to this lost wonder: a bronze signet ring depicting Pharos.

The ring is the “first of its kind known to exist,” the European Institute for Underwater Archaeology (IEASM) notes in a statement. Its design bears resemblance to portrayals of the lighthouse on Egyptian coins from the second century C.E. As archaeologist Isabelle Hairy writes for the Center for Alexandrian Studies, ancient currency offers “the most important documentary evidence” of Pharos’ appearance, suggesting that it had three tiers, including a square base, an octagonal middle section and a circular top. (Ancient writers left behind descriptions of the lighthouse, but these accounts are often conflicting, resulting in varying visual interpretations by later artists.)
Need to know: Wonders of the ancient world

- The structures most often cited as the seven wonders of the ancient world are the Great Pyramid of Giza, the Colossus of Rhodes, the Lighthouse of Alexandria, the Mausoleum at Halicarnassus, the Temple of Artemis at Ephesus, the Statue of Zeus at Olympia and the Hanging Gardens of Babylon.
- Of these seven, only the Great Pyramid of Giza survives today.

Researchers from the institute recovered the ring as part of a joint archaeological mission with the Egyptian Ministry of Tourism and Antiquities. According to a Facebook post shared by the ministry, archaeologists at the site have also found tableware, amphorae, oil lamps and fragments of glassware spanning the fourth century B.C.E. through the fourth century C.E.

“The discovery … is even more important, as [the ring] has been excavated in the legendary palace of the island of Antirhodos, that once upon a time was a center of power,” says Franck Goddio, IEASM’s founder and president, in the statement. The Greek geographer Strabo, who visited Alexandria in the first century B.C.E., described Antirhodos as “an isle lying off the artificial harbor, which has both a royal palace and a small harbor.” Its name, he added, was an allusion to its status as “a rival” of the Greek island of Rhodes.

For now, much about the ring remains unknown. “The statement does not say who wore this ring or what for,” Guillermo Carvajal writes for La Brújula Verde. “It gives neither its size nor its exact date.”

Still, the jewelry’s presence at the site has led the researchers to posit that the island once housed administrative offices designated for such tasks as management of the lighthouse. In ancient Egypt, bureaucrats used signet rings to sign legal documents; the pricey accessories also advertised their owners’ elite social status.

Construction of the lighthouse probably began during the reign of Ptolemy I Soter, a Macedonian general of Alexander the Great who served as Egypt’s first Ptolemaic king, and wrapped up under his son Ptolemy II Philadelphus, who succeeded him upon his death in 282 B.C.E. The Greek architect Sostratus of Cnidos designed the revolutionary structure, which is often described as the world’s first recorded lighthouse.

Today, physical evidence of Pharos is limited largely to stone blocks and metal clamps used to bind these blocks together. “The architectural fragments lie scattered over 18 acres underwater,” Hairy told the New York Times’ Franz Lidz earlier this year. “The visibility is extremely bad, the seabed is uneven and there are no clear layers of sediment.”

These challenges haven’t stopped Hairy and her colleagues at the Pharos Project from embarking on a multidisciplinary effort to reconstruct the ancient wonder digitally, piecing together photogrammetry scans of the lighthouse’s sparse ruins to envision what it might have looked like in its heyday.

Although Hairy estimates that the work is “still generations from completion,” per the Times, the project’s findings are poised to transform historians’ understanding of the fabled lighthouse. Until then, those hoping to see Pharos for themselves need look no further than the newly discovered ring.

Throughout world wars, pandemics and the turn of centuries, there was Jonathan. As the world around him shifted and changed, he lived the slow life munching grass on Saint Helena, a British island territory some 1,200 miles off the western coast of Africa.

The Aldabra giant tortoise is the oldest turtle in recorded history and the world’s oldest living land animal. Caretakers don’t know his exact age, but a photograph from 1882 shows the tortoise looking fully grown, which, for his species, is at least 50 years old. This means that Jonathan would be about 194 today.
“To be honest, I suspect he’s older,” veterinarian Joe Hollins, who looks after Jonathan, told the Washington Post’s Cathy Free in 2022. “But we can never know.”

No matter Jonathan’s exact age, one thing seems certain: Something has made him exceptional when it comes to withstanding the test of time. He has already lived more than a century beyond his species’ 80-year average life expectancy—a feat that his safe environment, diet and medical care alone might not be able to explain.

In a new study published on Wednesday in Science Advances, researchers examined Jonathan’s DNA for genetic clues to his extraordinary age. To collect the data, Hollins propped Jonathan’s mouth open with a gloved finger and swabbed a sample of cheek cells and saliva.

“We almost never get to study an animal this old while it is still alive,” says co-author Steve Horvath, a biologist who studies aging at the University of California, Los Angeles, to the New York Times’ Monique Brouillette.
Key context: False reports of Jonathan’s death

In April, false reports that Jonathan had died were circulated widely, stemming from a fake X post claiming to be the tortoise’s veterinarian. It turned out to be a hoax—a ploy for cryptocurrency donations.

The research team sequenced Jonathan’s DNA and identified 287 genetic variants that were unique to him. Many of these had to do with repairing damage to DNA, reducing inflammation and managing insulin. They also found that he shared aging-related genes with species including naked mole-rats, which almost never get cancer.

Additionally, they looked at Jonathan’s epigenome, the chemical tags on DNA that turn certain genes on and off. As organisms age, these switches become less predictable—tags might inconsistently attach or fall off, leading to erratic activity from genes. The team compared Jonathan’s epigenome with those of four younger tortoises.

Overall, Jonathan showed the chaos, or entropy, in the epigenome that would be expected for his age. But in the areas of the genome linked to things like DNA repair and mitochondria, the energy-producing centers in cells, Jonathan’s chemical tags were especially youthful. At these spots, Jonathan’s epigenome looked similar to DNA from a 5-year-old juvenile tortoise that the researchers studied.

The work doesn’t prove that these markers are the reason for Jonathan’s long life, but they offer a clue to how DNA might endure for long periods. They also align with findings from supercentenarians, humans who have lived to be more than 110 years old.

“Aging is the greatest risk factor for nearly every chronic disease we face,” study co-author Stephen Clark, founder and chief scientist at the nonprofit Kallel Foundation for aging research, says in a statement. “Our goal is to take these evolutionary insights and immediately translate them into practical, affordable treatments for everyday people.”

But before any of this information can find a medical use, scientists will have to conduct deeper research. For one, Jonathan’s cheek swab contained incomplete DNA, so the team combined his genome with a younger tortoise’s DNA, resulting in a code that was only about 95 percent Jonathan—and allowing for the possibility that some of his unique DNA variants were not included in the sample. A blood test would have produced a full genome, but because of the risk of infection for the tortoise, Saint Helena officials did not allow it.

What’s more, Jonathan is just one study subject, and it’s difficult to generalize any results based on a lone individual. His genome was also compared against only a small handful of other tortoises, as bioinformatics researcher Kousuke Hashimoto of the University of Osaka, Japan, tells New Scientist’s James Woodford, inviting the possibility that the other tortoises also had unique variants that were not identified. Nevertheless, he calls the study “fascinating.”

“The results integrate very well in the wider puzzle of what longevity is,” Björn Schumacher, who studies aging at the University of Cologne in Germany and was not involved in the study, tells the New York Times.

Jonathan was born in the Seychelles, an island nation in the Western Indian Ocean. But as a gift to the governor, he was brought to Saint Helena in 1882, when he was photographed as an adult. Since then, he has been living at Plantation House, the governor’s home, with other giant tortoises.

Hollins took charge of Jonathan’s care in 2009, when the animal was around 180 years old and not in great shape. Among markers of age, such as cataracts and a loss of smell that prevented him from finding his own food, the tortoise suffered from a soft beak that made it hard to graze. The veterinarian hand-fed Jonathan, who recovered and developed a razor-sharp edge to his beak within the next couple of years.
“He is symbolic of resilience, longevity, endurance,” Hollins tells Reuters’ Marta Serafinko, “a persistent presence throughout huge historic events.”
Oct. 9 (UPI) -- New York Jets running back Breece Hall and wide receiver Adonai Mitchell are ruled out for Week 5's game against the Cleveland Browns, coach Aaron Glenn told reporters Friday.
Glenn also said that left guard Dylan Parham and linebacker Kiko Mauigoa will not play Sunday.

Hall, who sustained a quadriceps injury in Week 3, would miss his second consecutive game. Mitchell missed the last two weeks due to a finger injury. Parham and Mauigoa are out with respective knee and quad injuries.

Second-string running back Braelon Allen started in place of Hall in the Jets' 23-12 loss to the Chicago Bears on Sunday in Chicago. He was in for 30 (94%) of the Jets' offensive snaps and totaled 67 yards from scrimmage off 16 touches. No other Jets running back logged a rushing attempt against the Bears.
Hall, who hasn't practiced since Week 3, totaled 265 yards from scrimmage and a score through his first three appearances this season.

Mitchell caught nine passes for 123 yards through his two appearances this season. The Jets started Garrett Wilson and Isaiah Williams at wide receiver over the last two weeks. Jordan Meredith filled in for Parham at left guard.

Glenn said defensive back Jarvis Brownlee, who is in the concussion protocol, is progressing well. Tight end Mason Taylor, who missed the last two games due to a thumb injury, is set to return in Week 5.
The Jets (1-3) will host the Browns (3-1) at 1 p.m. EDT Sunday in East Rutherford, N.J.
Oct. 9 (UPI) -- Hundreds of Marvel fans donned Spider-Man costumes at New York Comic Con in an attempt to break a Guinness World Record.

The Thursday event, organized by toy company Jazwares in collaboration with Disney Consumer Products, attempted to break the Guinness World Record for the largest gathering of people dressed as Spider-Man.
Organizers have not yet released an official count from the event, but acknowledged the final tally was just short of the current record of 685 participants.
The current record was set by Sony Pictures Entertainment Malaysia in 2023 to celebrate the theatrical release of Spider-Man: Across the Spider-Verse.
